nameStory: The Furry Snake Millipede gets its common name from its distinctive hairy appearance and snake-like movement as it glides through leaf litter. Unlike smooth millipedes, this species is covered in fine bristles that give it a fuzzy, almost woolly texture that's quite noticeable when you spot one.
description: The Furry Snake Millipede is a cylindrical, worm-like creature that's actually an arthropod, not a worm at all. These millipedes are covered in fine hairs that make them look distinctly fuzzy compared to their smooth relatives. They're typically brown to dark brown in color and can grow to about 1-2 inches long. As true millipedes, they have many pairs of legs (though not actually a thousand!) and move with a characteristic wave-like motion.

idTips.label: Fuzzy texture
idTips.description: The entire body is covered in fine, bristle-like hairs that you can see with the naked eye, giving it a distinctly furry appearance that feels slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Cylindrical body
idTips.description: Long, round, and worm-like with a consistent diameter throughout, about as thick as a pencil when fully grown

idTips.label: Brown coloration
idTips.description: Ranges from light brown to dark chocolate brown, sometimes with slightly lighter bands between body segments

idTips.label: Many legs
idTips.description: Two pairs of short legs per body segment create a rippling wave motion when walking, quite different from the side-to-side movement of centipedes

idTips.label: Coiling behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, curls into a tight spiral like a watch spring, often remaining motionless until the threat passes

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Adults typically reach 1-2 inches in length, making them medium-sized among New England millipedes

habitat: Look for Furry Snake Millipedes in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under rotting logs, leaf litter, and decomposing organic matter. They prefer areas with rich, damp soil and are often found in the same spots as other decomposer organisms like sowbugs and earthworms. You'll have the best luck finding them in mature forests with plenty of fallen leaves and decaying wood.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms, often found under logs and stones as they emerge from winter refuges. This is a good time to spot them as they're moving more but leaf litter is still sparse.
seasonality.summer: Most active during warm, humid weather, especially after rain. Look for them in the evening or early morning when moisture levels are highest.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed heavily on newly fallen leaves. This is often the best season for observation as they're numerous and leaf litter provides ideal habitat.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, burrowed deep in soil or under thick organic matter. Occasionally found under logs on warmer winter days, but generally dormant.

funFact: Despite being called a 'snake' millipede, this fuzzy creature is more closely related to lobsters and spiders than to any snake or worm - they're all arthropods with jointed legs and segmented bodies!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with smooth millipedes, but the fuzzy hair covering makes identification straightforward - just look for that distinctive furry texture. Remember: if it's hairy, it's likely this species; if it's smooth and shiny, it's probably a different millipede entirely.
contextualKnowledge: As an introduced species from Europe, the Furry Snake Millipede is actually a relatively recent arrival to New England's forests, though it has established itself successfully in the ecosystem as a harmless decomposer.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ophyiulus species in our region, compare it to other millipedes in the family Julidae by looking for the distinctive hairy covering. Most other julid millipedes in New England are smooth and glossy, making the Furry Snake Millipede's fuzzy appearance quite distinctive. The hair coverage is really the key feature that sets it apart from all its millipede relatives.
